I
The story is a parable. What instruction does it convey?
One thing is quite clear: the rich man's invitation symbolizes
the call of God which goes forth to invite men to enter His
kingdom. The people invited-both those who were first
invited as also those who were called in later—are the men
to whom the call of God comes. And the hearers of the
parable are asked whether it will be with them as with those
who were first invited, who, because they did not hold
themselves in readiness, missed the joy of the banquet. The
tone of the parable is obviously not consoling and cheering.
It is not that the teller is primarily thinking of those who were
not originally invited and later were in fact summoned to
share in the joy of the feast. The tone is rather solemn and
threatening, as the conclusion plainly shows: "I tell you,
none of those men who were invited shall taste my banquet."
It is easy to understand the parable in relation to Jesus
and His time. The original guests are the pious members of
the Jewish people, to whom Jesus' call to penitence was so
often directed, and against whom His anger was so often
kindled. These were men who for long had had special
knowledge of God and His call; who for long had said "yes,
yes!" and who now when Jesus comes with the proclamation
that the time is fulfilled close their ears and harden their
hearts against Him, and from whom He turns away to go
to "tax collectors and sinners" who were willing to listen to
His voice.
But if Jesus is speaking to us to-day through this parable,
then He is summoning us also to consider whether we do
not belong to the category of the original guests, who have
long accepted God's call and God's invitation but who,
when the matter becomes serious, calling for decision in the
present moment, prefer to be absorbed in private affairs and
to despise God's summons.
